title: The history of shell
titleCn: 贝壳的历史：从珠宝到货币

paragraphs.text: Today we're going to look at something small, beautiful, and surprisingly important in human history: shells and the many roles they have played, from jewelry to money.
Shells have been used as personal decoration for a remarkably long time. We know that shells were used to make necklaces about two thousand years ago, and probably much earlier.
Some of the earliest shell jewelry ever found comes from archaeological sites in Mexico, where ancient craftsmen drilled and polished shells with astonishing skill.
What made a shell valuable? Appearance, mostly. Shells with a shiny interior were especially prized in jewelry because the inside of the shell, once polished, glows like pearl.
Shells were not only worn around the neck. They were also arranged in patterns to decorate clothing and textiles, sewn onto ceremonial robes as a display of wealth and status.
They had practical uses, too. In farming communities, shells were used as tools to separate corn kernels from the cob. The hard, curved edge of a large shell does the job surprisingly well.
Most fascinating of all is the cowrie shell, which was used as money in trade across Africa and Asia.
Cowries were durable, portable, and almost impossible to counterfeit.
With cowrie currency, the total weight of the shells showed their value. Merchants simply weighed a pile rather than counting individual shells.
Cowries also carried meaning. In jewelry, they symbolized fertility and prosperity, which is why they so often appear in bridal ornaments.
Two final curiosities. Shells carried home by pilgrims have been found in Northern Spain, marking the great medieval walking routes.
And in some Pacific cultures, shell piles were given to men on their wedding day as a symbol of their new responsibilities.
